mainText: Good morning. Here is your curated AI briefing for Sunday, August 2, 2026. Moonshot AI has released Kimi K3, a 2.8 trillion parameter model that is currently the largest open-weight system available. This matters because as models scale to multi-trillion parameter architectures, organizations require specialized infrastructure to host them. Amazon Web Services detailed earlier this week that Kimi K3 utilizes a Mixture of Experts architecture, which activates only 16 experts per token—approximately 104 billion parameters—to improve efficiency. This represents a 2.5x increase in scaling efficiency over its predecessor, Kimi K2. The model is built with Kimi Delta Attention and Gated Multi-Head Latent Attention, specifically designed for complex reasoning, long-horizon coding, and agentic workflows. To support this scale, AWS recommends hosting the model on p6-b300 instances, which feature eight NVIDIA B300 Blackwell Ultra graphics processing units. Because of the model's significant size and technical requirements, vLLM is the recommended serving engine, providing native support for the model’s MXFP4 quantization format. The model is currently available on Hugging Face. In other major developments, Google DeepMind introduced Gemini Robotics ER 2, a model designed to function as a high-level reasoning system for robots. By integrating with video feeds, the model enables robots to track progress on physical tasks, self-correct in real-time, and collaborate with other robots. Google reports that the model utilizes a bidirectional streaming endpoint to reduce latency, allowing robots to perform multi-step actions without significant pauses, overcoming the "stop-and-think" latency common in previous systems. The model includes "moment finding" and progress classification capabilities, allowing robots to verify the completion of physical tasks like tightening a light bulb. This technology is being made available to developers through the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Separately, OpenAI reported earlier this week that it successfully disrupted a Cambodia-based criminal operation that utilized ChatGPT to facilitate financial and romance scams. The network reportedly used the model to draft deceptive messages, create fake personas, and generate forged documents, such as passports and investment confirmations. The operation followed a cycle of outreach, emotional manipulation, and financial extraction. OpenAI identified the operation through signals provided by industry peers and subsequently banned the coordinated network of accounts. This incident highlights the ongoing challenges companies face regarding the misuse of large language models for organized, large-scale deception. Also this week, Amazon Bedrock announced the general availability of the OpenAI GPT-5.6 model family, which includes Sol, Terra, and Luna. The Sol model is intended for complex reasoning, Terra for production workloads, and Luna for high-volume tasks. Alongside these models, Amazon introduced an explicit prompt caching capability, allowing developers to reuse specific portions of their prompts across multiple requests. AWS notes that cached inputs are billed at a 90 percent discount and remain available for 30 minutes, a feature intended to reduce costs for high-volume agentic workflows where tool definitions and system instructions are frequently repeated. In research, Microsoft released two new initiatives aimed at improving how agents function. The first, Echoverse, provides a collection of simulated environments for training computer-use agents, focusing on complex user interface elements like nested filters and date pickers. By using high-fidelity simulations that maintain state across interactions, Microsoft found that training agents in deep, realistic worlds significantly improves performance on real-world applications. The second, EvoLib, is a framework designed to enable models to learn from past experiences during inference without requiring full model updates. EvoLib extracts successful strategies from previous tasks and refines them into reusable knowledge, allowing models to improve performance over time through self-supervision and knowledge consolidation. Additionally, OpenAI affirmed its commitment to the European Union’s AI Act earlier this week.
